# George Dreemer — Data Scientist, Developer and Entrepreneur

Excellence through action.    Creatio Perpetua.

George Dreemer is a serial entrepreneur working across full-stack development, data science, and web3. His ventures range from an open-source Python library and a knowledge-first social network to an underground streetwear brand with thousands of fans.

That range is reflected in his toolkit: multi-language development, statistical modelling and machine learning, alongside years of hands-on work with Adobe, e-commerce platforms, and marketing analytics. He connects the technical build with the product, brand, and business around it.

His education spans Europe and the US, with an MSc in Marketing Analytics & Data Science and a BA in Marketing & Business. Completed tracks and certificates from DataCamp, Google, and research-training programmes complement that foundation.

# BA Marketing & Business — Hampshire College

George's BA at Hampshire College was a four-year, self-designed program focused on marketing, business, and entrepreneurship.

The curriculum connected marketing and consumer behaviour, business fundamentals, and persuasive communication: learning to research markets, assess business opportunities, negotiate agreements, and develop the strategy and visual identity behind a venture.

Through the Five College Consortium, George took accounting at Smith College and graduate-level coursework in Internet Business, Business Law, and Negotiation Theory & Practice at UMass Amherst's Isenberg School of Management. Alongside coursework and independent studies, George built the streetwear brand SkipSchoolMakeMoney and served on Hampshire's student-run Seed Fund for Innovation, evaluating venture pitches and voting on funding decisions.

## Degree Snapshot

**Degree:** Marketing & Business

**Type:** Bachelor of Arts (BA)

**Result:** 3.81 / 4.0

Estimated GPA

Hampshire evaluates its courses through written narrative evaluations, not letter grades, and does not issue an official GPA.

**Calculation:** My grade summary estimates a GPA by treating successfully completed Hampshire courses as A grades and combining them with the letter grades earned through the Five College Consortium.

Source: [Hampshire's guidance on estimated GPAs](<https://www.hampshire.edu/sites/default/files/centralrecords/Info%20GPA%20application.pdf>).

# MSc Marketing Analytics & Data Science — University of Groningen

George's MSc in Marketing Analytics & Data Science at the University of Groningen was a graduate program focused on applied statistics, machine learning, data science, and data engineering.

The program covered the full path from research design and data preparation to modelling, evaluation, and communication: statistical analysis, supervised learning, segmentation, text mining, sentiment analysis, time-series work, and business-facing decision support across consumer and retail contexts.

In practice, George used Python and R for modelling, data wrangling, and automation, and Stata and SPSS for statistical testing and survey-style analysis. He used SQL for data engineering and extraction, and turned the results into data visualizations, written reports, and presentations. The code, reports, and slides behind the theses and projects are publicly browsable, with the programming linked through George's GitHub.

## Degree Snapshot

University of Groningen

University of Groningen   \#84 World (ARWU)   \#46 Business (ARWU)

University of Groningen — world rankings

- **\#84** ARWU Shanghai Ranking; Business Administration **\#46**

- **\#87** Times Higher Education; Business & Economics **\#69**

- **\#6** UI GreenMetric, sustainability

University-level rankings, not specific to this programme. Source: [RUG](<https://www.rug.nl/about-ug/profile/facts-and-figures/position-international-rankings?lang=en>)

**Degree:** Marketing Analytics & Data Science

**Type:** Master of Science (MSc)

**Result:** 8 / 10

Dutch grading scale

Average grade across the whole programme. The separate thesis grade is an 8.

**Context:** At UG only about 14% of single-grades awarded are an 8 and 2.7% are a 9.

Source: [RUG](<https://www.rug.nl/education/student-blog/what-dutch-grades-actually-mean-24-01-2020?lang=en>).

**Faculty:** Faculty of Economics and Business

**Location:** Groningen, Netherlands

**Links:** [Official program page](<https://www.rug.nl/masters/msc-marketing-marketing-analytics-and-data-science/?lang=en>)

### Written reports

Documents showcasing academic and corporate reporting.

[Pre-MSc thesis: Earnings call sentiment and stock volatility](<https://www.canva.com/design/DAF05sFmKwQ/view?embed>)

Data Pre-MSc Thesis

#### Earnings Call Sentiment & Stock Volatility

- Asked whether the sentiment of an earnings call shapes how volatile a stock is afterwards, using 178 call transcripts from 10 NASDAQ-listed firms.

- Cleaned the transcripts and scored them with NLTK's VADER, then scraped stock and NASDAQ index prices for the 10 days either side of each call to measure the change in volatility, and tested sentiment with multiple linear regression.

- Volatility rose after 87% of calls, yet sentiment was not a statistically significant predictor. The paper reports this plainly and points to other factors worth testing, while showing the call itself is a decisive moment for volatility.

## Thesis

MSc thesis · University of Groningen · Grade: 8 / 10

### Willingness to Share Health Data in Italy: Investigation under a Multi-context Paradigm with DCE Data

Synopsis:

What makes people willing to share their health data beyond its original use? I analysed choices from 329 respondents in Italy to understand how the organisations involved, the intended use, consent arrangements, and external oversight shape that decision.

[Read the full paper](<https://georgedreemer.com/downloads/academic/georgedreemer-msc-thesis_paper.pdf>) [Defence slides](<https://georgedreemer.com/downloads/academic/georgedreemer-msc-thesis_defenseslides.pdf>) [Analysis code](<https://github.com/ETA444/msc_mads/tree/main/theses>)

**Participants:** 329 in Italy

**Latent preference groups:** 2 46.5% / 53.5% of respondents

**Contextual attributes:** 5 examined together

**Analysis tools:** R & Stata 17

**Research question:** How do different data-sharing arrangements influence willingness to allow the secondary use of health data?

Five contextual attributes were examined together:

- Original data collector

- New data user

- Purpose of reuse

- Information & consent

- External review

**Analytical approach:** I analysed discrete-choice-experiment data supplied by Biasiotto and colleagues: 329 participants in Italy.

1. Compared five models in Stata (three latent class specifications, a conditional logit, and a logistic regression), judging fit by AIC and log-likelihood.

2. Interpreted a two-class latent class model as the primary analysis, with the conditional logit as a secondary check.

3. Calculated average relative attribute importance from the primary model.

**Finding & relevance:** Respondents leaned toward not sharing, but context shifted that.

Two preference groups (46.5% and 53.5%) ranked the five attributes identically:

1. Who reuses the data

2. Purpose of reuse

3. Information about sharing

4. Review of the transfer

5. Original data collector

Yet they preferred different options within each attribute. On who reuses the data, their orders were contrasting. One-size-fits-all rules are therefore unlikely to fit, while transparency and some form of external review were common ground.

Inside the experiment

#### Same health data. Different sharing context.

A willingness-to-share decision involves more than the data itself. Change who collected it, who wants to reuse it, why, and under which safeguards. These were the five contextual attributes examined together in the research.

Build a sharing context

Choose an option for each attribute. The context summary updates automatically.

Original data collector

New data user

Purpose of reuse

Information and consent

External review

Illustrative context

Imagine your health data being reused under these arrangements:

**Originally collected by:** Healthcare provider

**Reused by:** National authority

**Used for:** Quality evaluation

**Information and consent:** Informed, with ability to opt in

**External review:** Review of data transfer and use

Would these arrangements change your willingness to share?

The study asked participants to accept or reject sharing across varying contexts. This explorer illustrates the attributes; it does not record your answer or estimate a sharing probability.

Educational reconstruction using the study’s attribute levels—not a reproduction of an original choice task. Combinations selected here are not necessarily among the scenarios administered in the study.

What the analysis revealed

#### Two groups agreed on what matters, and disagreed on what they prefer.

Overall, respondents leaned toward not sharing. Willingness depended on the arrangement, and the five attributes did not carry equal weight.

Importance of the five attributes

1. New data user

2. Reason for new data use

3. Information & consent

4. External review

5. Original data collector

Ranking based on average relative attribute importance in the primary two-class latent class model. Both modelled groups shared the same attribute-importance order, while differing in their preferred levels within several attributes.

Figure 6 Average relative attribute importance

Image: [Figure 6. Average relative importance of the five contextual attributes.](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-figure6.png>)

As reported in the thesis: the new data user and the reason for reuse carry the most weight, followed by information and consent.

 [Open full size ↗](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-figure6.png>)

An expectation challenged

I expected information & consent to be the most influential attribute and the reason for reuse to rank second. The second expectation held; the first did not. The new data user ranked first and information & consent third, so who receives the data mattered more than how consent is organised.

Inside the two groups

#### One country, two contrasting preference patterns.

The latent class model split respondents into two groups, 46.5% and 53.5%. Pick an attribute to compare how each group ordered its levels, from highest to lowest estimated utility.

##### New data user · importance rank 1 of 5

Group 1 46.5% of respondents

1. Technological company

2. National authority reference level

3. Pharmaceutical company

4. Academic research project

Group 2 53.5% of respondents

1. Academic research project

2. Pharmaceutical company

3. National authority reference level

4. Technological company

##### Reason for new data use · importance rank 2 of 5

Group 1 46.5% of respondents

1. Investigating a policy initiative

2. Quality evaluation reference level

3. Promotion, advertising or marketing

4. Developing a new product or service

Group 2 53.5% of respondents

1. Developing a new product or service

2. Quality evaluation reference level

3. Promotion, advertising or marketing

4. Investigating a policy initiative

##### Information & consent · importance rank 3 of 5

Group 1 46.5% of respondents

1. Informed only, no consent option

2. Informed, with ability to opt in reference level

3. Not informed

4. Informed, with ability to opt out

Group 2 53.5% of respondents

1. Informed, with ability to opt out

2. Informed, with ability to opt in reference level

3. Informed only, no consent option

4. Not informed

##### External review · importance rank 4 of 5

Group 1 46.5% of respondents

1. Review of data transfer and use reference level

2. No review

3. Review of data transfer only

Group 2 53.5% of respondents

1. Review of data transfer only

2. No review

3. Review of data transfer and use reference level

##### Original data collector · importance rank 5 of 5

Group 1 46.5% of respondents

1. Academic research project

2. Technological company

3. Healthcare provider reference level

Group 2 53.5% of respondents

1. Healthcare provider reference level

2. Technological company

3. Academic research project

Levels are ordered by each group’s estimated utility. The order does not show how large the gaps are or whether neighbouring levels differ significantly; those details are in Table 4. For the original collector, new data user, and external review attributes, the groups displayed substantially contrasting orderings. Group 1 placed technological companies first as the new data user, a pattern that differs from much earlier research but resembles a Southern European subgroup reported by Biasiotto et al.

Table 4 2-class latent class model with initial values

Image: [Table 4. Results of the 2-class latent class model estimated with initial values.](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-table4.png>)

Scroll sideways to see the full table.

 [Open full size ↗](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-table4.png>)

What it suggests

#### Plan for different audiences, not one average citizen.

The two groups' contrasting preferences sit alongside a shared emphasis on transparency and oversight.

**Expect heterogeneity inside a country:** Within one Italian sample, two groups held contrasting preferences on most attributes. A single average preference would have hidden that.

**Be cautious about one-size-fits-all rules:** Some results differ from larger multinational studies. That suggests data-reuse policy may not fit every European region equally, and that country-specific consideration and research are worthwhile.

**Treat transparency and review as common ground:** Being informed and having some form of external review matched earlier research. In both groups, the most preferred information arrangement was an informed one, and the most preferred review option was some form of review. This supports transparency, clarity of purpose and independent oversight as institutional practice.

These are research-informed considerations, not a tested intervention or a demonstrated increase in real-world sharing.

For a closer look

#### Research decisions and supporting evidence

Explore how the sample was prepared, how the preference models were specified, and where the interpretation needs care.

Sample, data checks, and descriptive analysis

929 survey initiations, 362 completions, and 329 respondents after removing completions under five minutes.

Before modelling I checked for missing values and outliers. No variable had more than 3.95% missing values, and none were independent variables. Thirty-four respondents had unusually long completion times (over 30 minutes). I reviewed their written feedback, found nothing abnormal, and discussed the pattern with my supervisor. The survey software let people pause and resume, so I did not treat the durations as a data-quality problem.

The final sample had a mean age of 50.83 years (SD 14.55), was 53% female and 47% male, and was most often educated to high-school level (42.1%) or master's level (about 27%). 54.6% reported no chronic condition, and 32.1% had sufficient eHealth literacy (37.6% problematic, 30.3% inadequate).

Fieldwork, recruitment and the experimental design were carried out by the source research team.

Figure 3 Missing-value summary

Image: [Figure 3. Summary of missing values in the dataset.](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-figure3.png>)

 [Open full size ↗](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-figure3.png>)

Figure 5 Health-related descriptives

Image: [Figure 5. Descriptive statistics on respondents' health-related characteristics.](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-figure5.png>)

 [Open full size ↗](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-figure5.png>)

How the choice experiment worked

The source experiment used 32 unique choice tasks, arranged into four blocks of eight. Each participant completed two sets of eight decisions, covering two assigned health-information themes from lifestyle, physical health, mental health, and genetic information.

Each task presented a sharing context. Participants decided whether to accept or reject sharing under those arrangements, rather than selecting a favourite organisation or purpose in isolation.

This structure enabled the analysis to examine contextual trade-offs across the five attributes. The health-information themes are part of the experimental setting; they are not an additional attribute in the five-factor explorer above.

Sixteen decisions per participant are repeated observations from the same people—not sixteen independent respondents.

Figure 2 Example choice task

Image: [Figure 2. Example choice task from the study: a table showing one data-sharing scenario with a level for each of the five attributes, which participants accepted or rejected.](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-figure2-choicetask.png>)

Scroll sideways to see the full figure.

 [Open full size ↗](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-figure2-choicetask.png>)

Model selection and attribute importance

After checking correlations between the independent variables for multicollinearity, I fitted five models of three types in Stata 17: three latent class models (one class; two classes without starting values; two classes with starting values from the one-class model), a conditional logit, and a logistic regression. I compared them by AIC and log-likelihood.

Table 3 AIC and log-likelihood for the five models

Image: [Table 3. AIC and log-likelihood values for the five fitted models.](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-table3.png>)

 [Open full size ↗](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-table3.png>)

The two best-fitting models were the two-class latent class model with starting values and the conditional logit. I treated the former as the primary analysis and the latter as a secondary check. A latent class model divides respondents into classes by their expressed preferences instead of assuming one common pattern; the conditional logit assumes a common utility function, a limitation the latent class model addresses.

Average relative attribute importance was computed in three steps:

1. For each attribute, subtract its lowest level estimate from its highest to get a range.

2. Divide each range by the largest range, giving relative importance per attribute within each class.

3. Average the values across the two classes.

Equation Latent class model

Image: [Equation for the latent class model, as specified in the thesis.](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-equation-latentclassmodel.png>)

Scroll sideways to see the full equation.

 [Open full size ↗](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-equation-latentclassmodel.png>)

Equation Conditional logit model

Image: [Equation for the conditional logit model, as specified in the thesis.](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-equation-conditionallogitmodel.png>)

Scroll sideways to see the full equation.

 [Open full size ↗](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-equation-conditionallogitmodel.png>)

Primary results: the two-class model

All five attributes were statistically significant in the primary model. Estimated group shares were 46.5% and 53.5%. Both groups showed a general disutility for sharing, with positive rejection intercepts of 0.48 and 0.59 (both p \< 0.001).

- **Shared ranking:** both groups gave the same importance ranking: new data user, reason, information & consent, review, original collector.

- **Different levels:** groups differed on which level they preferred within each attribute, and their orders were exact reverses on collector, recipient and review.

- **Common features:** neither group ranked opt-in consent first, and both groups' top review option was some form of review.

Significance of individual levels within each group is reported in Table 4. Latent classes are model-based preference patterns, not observed personality types.

Secondary results: the conditional logit check

Eight of the thirteen estimated levels were significant (pseudo R² 0.111; LR chi² 410.87, p \< .001). Compared with the reference levels, and holding other variables constant:

- **Original collector:** sharing was less likely when it was a technology company than a healthcare provider; an academic project was not significant (p = 0.970).

- **New data user:** no level was significant.

- **Reason:** product or service development raised the likelihood of sharing and marketing lowered it, relative to quality evaluation.

- **Information & consent:** informed-only and informed-with-opt-out raised it relative to opt-in, and not being informed lowered it.

- **Review:** review of transfer only raised it relative to review of transfer and use, and no review lowered it.

Conditional logit coefficients give direction, not the size of differences between levels, so this model corroborates the latent class results without replacing them.

Table 5 Conditional logit results

Image: [Table 5. Results of the conditional logit model.](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-table5-conditionallogitmodel.png>)

Scroll sideways to see the full table.

 [Open full size ↗](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/education/mscthesis/mscthesis-table5-conditionallogitmodel.png>)

Limitations and what comes next

- **Sample composition:** education was uneven (42.1% high school, about 27% master's, other levels around 10% or less). Earlier research links education to data-sharing attitudes, so the preferences may mainly describe these education groups. A more balanced sample could yield more classes or different preferences.

- **Timing:** fieldwork ran during the COVID-19 aftermath. Earlier research suggests the pandemic raised willingness to share, so comparisons across time periods would be useful.

- **No covariates:** the latent class model includes none. Age, trust, and privacy and technology attitudes from the survey are natural next additions. One idea is to cluster respondents on trust and privacy attitudes and use those clusters as covariates.

- **Stated choices:** the experiment measures decisions in described scenarios, not real transfers of health records.

- **Scope:** the findings inform governance considerations; they are not a legal-compliance assessment or proof that a policy would increase sharing.

See the defence slides

The slides I used to present the research question, modelling approach, and findings to the Committee at my Thesis Defence.

# CryptoPandemic — Web3 Marketing & On-Chain Analytics on Solana

CryptoPandemic is a Web3 brand engine built on one conviction: the projects that spread are not the ones with the best technology. They are the ones with the strongest story, the sharpest identity, and content that moves at the speed of the culture.

CryptoPandemic brings together two seemingly opposite forces: cold on-chain analytics and warm creative storytelling. The on-chain data acts as the "KYC", revealing exactly who your holders are, which coins they move, and what makes them act. The creative work responds to that data through a crypto cartoon series and visual identity built around the people already in your corner.

The approach was first applied to $BULLISH on Solana — crypto cartoon series, AI-generated content pipelines, 360° brand execution, on-chain market research — all deployed in tandem. The result was a market cap move from ~$6–7M to a peak of ~$13M, 5K+ daily mentions across Crypto Twitter, and 250K+ impressions across content.

## Experience Snapshot

Crypto Pandemic

**Role:** Founder & Creative Director

**Type:** Web3 Brand Studio

**Links:** [cryptopandemic.com](<https://cryptopandemic.com>)

### Highlights

- Profiled on-chain holder behaviour to identify the most effective branding styles and content formats

- Tracked X sentiment and news cycles to time and shape cryptoon storylines

- Coined the "cryptoon" format — narrative-driven crypto animations built on sentiment and on-chain data

- Created 50+ branded assets adopted by the community across X, Telegram, and Discord

- Drove Bullish from ~$6M to $13M peak market cap through coordinated cryptoon drops and brand strategy

- Drove 250K+ cross-platform impressions and 5K+ daily mentions

- Built AI-generative content pipelines and brand tools using Google AI Studio

# DataSafari — Open-Source Python Library for Data Science

DataSafari is a Python library that simplifies complex data science tasks — compressing exploration, transformation, evaluation, and prediction into a single one-liner API. One import. One function call. One plain-English report.

George built DataSafari to solve a specific problem he watched play out at university: data science curricula built around Stata, R, and SPSS — tools with decades of academic inertia — while Python's better-maintained, faster, and more capable ecosystem went largely untaught. The researcher who understands their domain deeply but doesn't want to spend two hours reading Scipy docs to run a single test was the exact person the existing tooling failed. DataSafari is the attempt to fix that: one import, one function call, one plain-English report.

The library spans four subpackages — Explorer, Transformer, Evaluator, Predictor — mirroring the natural stages of any data workflow. Every function handles its stage end-to-end: automatic statistical method selection, dynamic assumption validation, composite-score model evaluation. Each call returns a plain-language report with findings and actionable recommendations — results that are interpretable, not just computed.

## Experience Snapshot

Data Safari

**Role:** Creator & Maintainer

**Type:** Data Science Python Library

**Links:** [Website](<https://datasafari.dev>)
 [Docs](<https://datasafari.dev/docs>)
 [GitHub](<https://github.com/ETA444/datasafari>)
 [PyPI](<https://pypi.org/project/datasafari/>)

### Highlights

- Architected 4-subpackage API from scratch: Explorer · Transformer · Evaluator · Predictor

- Unified 10 scientific libraries — NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, scipy, statsmodels & more — into a single one-liner workflow

- Implemented automatic statistical test routing in predict\_hypothesis() — detects variable types, checks assumptions, selects and runs the correct test

- Built composite-score ML model evaluation engine with automated hyperparameter tuning in predict\_ml()

- Implemented statistical assumption checking across normality, variance, dtype, and contingency in Evaluator

- Designed multi-method outlier detection covering Z-score, IQR & Mahalanobis distance in Explorer

- Engineered 250+ pytest tests across 11 test files covering all 4 subpackages

- Built full GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline: lint · test · security scan · build · docs deploy · publish

- Configured CI matrix to run across Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11 & 3.12 in parallel

- Secured codebase with Bandit static scanning and SafetyCLI dependency auditing

- Tracked and closed 136 GitHub issues across the full development lifecycle

- Packaged and published to PyPI via an automated Poetry + Twine pipeline

- Automated Sphinx docs build and live-server deployment via rsync over SSH on every push

- Authored full Sphinx documentation site with custom Furo theme at datasafari.dev/docs

- Designed and launched dedicated product website at datasafari.dev

## In Numbers

**10+:** Pipeline decisions automated per ML run

**666:** Commits pushed

### Defensive Python & Input Validation

Domain: engineering

Ability description:

Implemented rigorous input validation and error handling across all 11 public functions. Each accepts DataFrames, column names, and optional parameter combinations that can fail silently in naive code. I built runtime branching logic to detect data types, sample sizes, and edge cases, then route execution to the correct algorithm path. Every error message is written for the caller, not the developer. In an API, the message *is* the UI & UX together.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Defensive Programming

- Runtime Type Handling

- Error Design

### Exploratory Data Analysis Systems

Domain: data

Ability description:

Designed and implemented the full Explorers subpackage. `explore_df()` profiles datasets, `explore_num()` performs numerical analysis including outlier detection via Z-score, IQR, and Mahalanobis distance, and `explore_cat()` profiles categorical data, including Shannon entropy to quantify diversity.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Exploratory Analysis

- Outlier Detection

- Statistical Profiling

### Statistical Assumption Verification

Domain: data

Ability description:

Built the Evaluators subpackage to automate the assumption checks that data scientists typically perform before analysis. `evaluate_normality()` selects an appropriate test, such as Shapiro-Wilk or Anderson-Darling, based on the sample; `evaluate_variance()` dynamically applies Levene's, Bartlett's, or Fligner's test; and `evaluate_contingency_table()` checks whether Chi-square conditions are met.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Assumption Testing

- Statistical Inference

- Dynamic Test Selection

### Automated Hypothesis Testing

Domain: data

Ability description:

`predict_hypothesis()` takes a DataFrame, a grouping variable, and a target variable — and autonomously selects and executes the correct statistical test. The function detects variable types, verifies normality and variance homogeneity, chooses between Chi-square, Fisher's exact, t-test, ANOVA, Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, and others, then outputs test statistics, p-values, and a plain-language interpretation.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Hypothesis Testing

- Automated Inference

- Statistical Interpretation

### End-to-End ML Pipeline Automation

Domain: data

Ability description:

`predict_ml()` orchestrates the complete machine learning workflow in one call — automatic preprocessing (scaling, encoding, vectorisation), multi-model evaluation using a user-configurable composite score weighted across multiple metrics, and automated hyperparameter tuning via grid search, random search, or Bayesian optimisation. Returns ranked, tuned models with full performance breakdowns.

Skills developed through this ability:

- ML Pipeline Design

- Hyperparameter Optimisation

- Model Selection

### Data Transformation Engineering

Domain: data

Ability description:

Implemented the Transformers subpackage to handle the full data preparation stage. `transform_num()` covers standardisation, min-max scaling, log and power transforms, winsorisation, and interaction term creation. `transform_cat()` handles label encoding, one-hot encoding, target encoding, and ML-based category cleaning — all chainable and parameterised for reproducible pipelines.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Feature Engineering

- Data Cleaning

- Preprocessing Pipeline Design

### Developer API & UX Design

Domain: product

Ability description:

Built datasafari around a deliberate developer experience philosophy — consistent naming across all 11 functions, predictable argument patterns, and sensible defaults that make the library immediately usable without reading the docs. Complex workflows like full ML pipelines and hypothesis testing are exposed as single function calls, hiding implementation complexity behind a clean interface.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Interface Design

- Developer Experience

- Abstraction Design

### Documentation Site Development

Domain: product

Designed and hand-coded datasafari.dev — the public documentation and landing site for the library. Built with custom HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, the site presents the library's philosophy, quick-start guides, and full API reference in a clean, readable format. Integrated with Sphinx and Read the Docs for automated doc generation, while the landing experience was crafted entirely from scratch.

Managed datasafari as a solo product owner, from its initial concept and roadmap through versioned releases, issue tracking, and ongoing maintenance. Data

### Automated EDA — `explore_num()`

- Single function call produces full numerical profiling: outlier detection via Z-score, IQR, and Mahalanobis distance, normality testing, skewness, kurtosis, and multicollinearity

- Output is a structured plain-English report with findings and actionable recommendations — not raw numbers

- Automatically selects the correct statistical method based on sample size and data characteristics at runtime

Data

### End-to-End ML Pipeline — `predict_ml()`

- One call handles preprocessing, multi-model training, composite-score-based evaluation weighted across user-configurable metrics, and ranked output

- Automated hyperparameter tuning via grid search, random search, or Bayesian optimisation — user selects strategy, library handles execution

- 10 pipeline decisions automated per ML run: encoding, scaling, model selection, tuning strategy, evaluation weighting, and recommendation generation

## In Depth

#### Built for the Professor Who Doesn't Have Time to Learn Python

At RUG, the standard data science curriculum ran on Stata, R, and SPSS. These tools have decades of academic inertia behind them, not necessarily because they are better, but because professors mastered them before Python became a serious data science platform and have not had time to switch. As a result, students graduate knowing tools that industry has largely moved beyond, while Python's better-maintained, faster, free, and more capable ecosystem goes untaught. Professors and other departmental staff have too much on their hands for a full curriculum redesign.

DataSafari started as a direct response to that gap. The hypothesis was simple: bring Python's best statistical and ML libraries together under a single interface that requires no configuration and produces plain-English output. That removes the adoption barrier for the person who most needs it: a researcher who knows their field, understands what a normality test is, but doesn't want to spend two hours reading `scipy.stats` documentation to run one. One import, one function call, and one readable report.

The iPhone analogy is imperfect but directionally useful. R is like Android: powerful, flexible, and beloved by people willing to configure it. DataSafari aims to provide an iOS-like layer on top of Python's underlying ecosystem.

That philosophy drove every product decision. It's why `method='all'` is the default rather than a required argument. It's why output is printed in plain English with interpretive tips instead of being returned as a raw matrix. It's why the function names are verbs such as `explore`, `transform`, `evaluate`, and `predict`. They describe what the user wants to do, not what the statistics are called. The target user was never a Python expert. It was someone who needed to do real data science work without letting the tooling become the hardest part of the day.

#### Input Engineering: Ask Less, Do More

The hardest design constraint in DataSafari was self-imposed: a user should be able to call any function with just a DataFrame and a column list and get something genuinely useful back. No configuration, statistical expertise, or output parsing should be required. The library decides the rest.

Making that work means every function carries a significant amount of internal decision-making that the user never sees. `explore_num()` takes a single `method` parameter that defaults to `'all'` — which means it runs correlation analysis, distribution analysis, three separate outlier detection algorithms (Z-score, IQR, and Mahalanobis distance), and a multicollinearity check in one call. The user passed two arguments. The library ran seven analyses and printed a structured plain-English report. That ratio — minimal input to maximal output — is the whole product.

But the API was also designed not to limit experts. Every function offers a full set of parameters for users who want to go deeper: `method='outliers_iqr'` to isolate a single analysis, `output='return'` to get structured DataFrames instead of printed text, and `threshold_z=2` to tighten the Z-score cutoff for a stricter definition of an outlier. The one-liner is the entry point; the parameters are the escape hatches. Designing that layered experience, where simple stays simple and complexity remains possible, required thinking through every plausible user intent before writing a single line of logic, then ensuring the implementation served them all without conflict.

#### Error Handling as User Experience

A Python traceback is the last thing a researcher wants to see at 11pm before a deadline. Every public function in DataSafari raises structured, specific errors before it does any computation — and the error messages are written for the person calling the function, not for the developer who wrote it.

The error handling layer sits entirely above the statistical logic. Before `explore_num()` touches a single column, it checks: is `df` actually a DataFrame? Is `numerical_variables` a list? Are the strings in that list real column names that exist in `df`? Are those columns actually numerical? Is the list non-empty? Is the DataFrame non-empty? Is `method` one of the seven valid options? Is `output` one of the two valid options? Is `threshold_z` a number? That's nine distinct failure modes caught and surfaced with a clear message and a correct-usage example — before a single line of analysis runs. Every one of those checks exists because someone, at some point during development and testing, made exactly that mistake.

The discipline behind this is that a library function has no UI. The error message *is* the UI. If a user passes a string where a list is expected and gets back `TypeError: 'str' object is not iterable`, that's a failed product moment — they have to reverse-engineer what went wrong from a generic Python exception. If they get back `"explore_num(): The numerical_variables parameter must be a list of variable names. Example: var_list = ['var1', 'var2', 'var3']"`, they fix it in ten seconds and move on. That difference is entirely a writing problem, not a coding one, and it took as much time to get right as the statistical methods themselves.

#### The Hidden 80%: What It Actually Takes to Ship a Python Package

The data science code, including the statistical methods, ML pipeline, and EDA logic, represents perhaps 20% of what it took to ship DataSafari. The other 80% consists of infrastructure decisions that tutorials rarely cover and that took weeks of research to get right.

The production configuration alone spans a dozen files beyond the package source itself:

- `pyproject.toml:` unified build, dependency, and tool configuration via Poetry and Setuptools

- `bumpversion.cfg:` automated semantic versioning with bump2version, wired to the CI pipeline to auto-increment on tagged releases

- `tox.ini:` multi-environment test runner across Python 3.9 to 3.12, so no version-specific regression ships undetected

- `setup.cfg` and `MANIFEST.in:` package inclusion rules to control exactly what ends up in the wheel and sdist

- `pyproject.toml:` Bandit config block, with the static security scan tuned to ignore specific false-positive patterns in the codebase

- `LICENSE:` GPL-3.0, chosen deliberately: use it freely, but derivatives stay open

- `Sphinx's conf.py:` the full documentation build configuration, including the Napoleon extension for Google-style docstrings, the Furo theme, and cross-reference resolution

Every one of those files required learning a tool I hadn't used before, reading its documentation, making it work with the others, and then making the entire stack reproducible in GitHub Actions. The CI pipeline didn't run cleanly on the first push or even the tenth. Over the development lifecycle, 136 issues were filed and closed, most of them documenting this kind of integration friction and its solution.

Documentation was another substantial layer of the work, especially the documentation users encounter inside the library: the `docstrings`. Every public function in DataSafari has a complete docstring with typed parameters, return types, raised exceptions, and a working code example that produces real output. More than 20 functions, including non-public ones, are documented to the point that `help(ds.explore_num)` gives a new user everything needed to use the function correctly without opening a browser. Writing that documentation took longer than writing some of the functions themselves.

# DREEMCORP — Creative Studio & Venture Lab

DREEMCORP is a creative studio specialized in photo and video editing, graphic design, personal branding, and social media strategy. George has worked with 12+ clients and brands and completed 100+ creative and marketing assignments.

The content across clients has been diverse, ranging from long-form YouTube edits to short-form TikTok and Instagram content, and from brand identity packages to social media strategy and consulting. Some of the clients include entertainers and athletes such as Najib Amhali, Amira Tahri, Alistair Overeem, and Frenna, alongside consumer brands like 92Minerals, Immersive Studios, and CoolSouls.

Across all platforms, these creations have reached 1M+ views and 100K+ likes and comments. George had the pleasure of working alongside visionary Younes Belguebli of YBI Media, an award-winning marketing and media agency in the Netherlands.

# SkipSchoolMakeMoney — Streetwear Brand

SkipSchoolMakeMoney (SSMM) was a streetwear brand born out of evening shifts at the Hampshire College media lab — no funding, no team, no formula. It grew from one hand-drawn logo into a cult-like following spanning three continents & hundreds of orders per collection.

SSMM was never just a clothing line. It was underground streetwear built on story, community, and relentless self-taught hustle — design, manufacturing, marketing, and logistics, all run by one person with a vision.

George designed and released 20+ collections, pioneered viral marketing methods amassing 12,000+ followers, and managed manufacturing pipelines spanning the US, UK, and China — earning recognition awards from startup accelerators and putting SSMM on the map of underground streetwear, music and meme culture.

## Experience Snapshot

SkipSchoolMakeMoney

**Role:** Founder, Designer & Operator

**Type:** Streetwear Apparel Brand

**Location:** Amherst, MA, United States

**Links:** [Official Webstore](<https://www.skipschoolmakemoney.com>)
 [Instagram Page](<https://www.instagram.com/skipschoolmakemoney>)

### Highlights

- Designed 20+ collections, amounting to 200+ individual designs

- Directed 25+ photo & video shoots across 6 countries — collaborating with photographers, models, and musicians

- Grew Instagram to 12,000+ followers at peak, driving 100s comments and 1000s of likes/post

- Pioneered guerilla Instagram growth strategies — including meme marketing, viral giveaways and influencer collaborations

- Ran paid ad campaigns across Instagram, Twitter, YouTube, and Snapchat

- Built and grew multiple Mailchimp mailing lists to 1000s of subscribers

- Negotiated promotional deals with influencers, media, and creators

- Managed manufacturing across the US West and East coasts, later expanding to the UK and China

- Organized supply chain, packaging, and shipping to serve customers across 3 continents

- Built 3 complete redesigns of the Shopify storefront end-to-end

- Built 2 complete redesigns of the Squarespace storefront end-to-end

- Integrated manufacturing and shipping APIs to automate order fulfillment and tracking

- Streamlined customer communications for abandoned carts, post-purchase follow-ups, and product launches

- Set up and maintained Shopify, Mailchimp, and Google Analytics for marketing, sales, and analytics

- Won the VVM Startup Accelerator Award, earning funding, mentorship, and resources

- Won the Grinspoon Recognition Award for Entrepreneurial Spirit

## In Numbers

**200+:** Designs released

**12K+:** Instagram followers at peak

**100K+:** Engagements generated

**1000+:** Orders fulfilled

## Abilities

Ability Domains

- Engineering

- Product

- Growth

- Data

### Brand & Collection Design

Domain: product

Ability description:

Built the SSMM identity from a single front-and-back logo into a full underground streetwear universe, designing and releasing 20+ collections that grew into several hundred individual graphics, garments, and visual concepts. Every drop had to feel culturally sharp, visually distinct, and native to the world of underground fashion, music, and meme culture.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Apparel Graphic Design

- Collection Development

- Production Coordination

### Viral Growth & Audience Building

Domain: growth

Ability description:

Grew SSMM to 12,000+ Instagram followers at peak by pioneering aggressive organic growth strategies built on meme marketing, giveaways, influencer collaborations, and constant experimentation with what actually triggered engagement. The result was a highly active audience that drove hundreds to thousands of comments per post, thousands of likes, and real demand across multiple drops.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Organic Growth Strategy

- Meme & Culture Marketing

- Campaign Automation

### Influencer, Music & Culture Positioning

Domain: growth

Ability description:

Built relationships across the underground creative scene, working with musicians, influencers, photographers, and content creators whose audiences aligned with the brand’s identity. Collaborations and organic placements with names like Lil Peep, Pouya, Fat Nick, CA$HRINA, Lil Johnnie, and others helped position SSMM inside the cultural conversation rather than outside it as just another apparel shop.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Influencer Outreach

- Partnership Development

- Cultural Positioning

### Creative Direction & Content Production

Domain: product

Ability description:

Directed 25+ photo and video shoots across six countries, coordinating photographers, models, locations, styling, and deliverables to give each collection a world around it. This turned SSMM from a product catalog into a lifestyle brand with visuals strong enough to travel across feeds, campaigns, and fan communities.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Production Coordination

- Photo & Video Editing

- Product Photography

- Campaign Asset Production

### Storefronts, Fulfillment & Commerce Ops

Domain: engineering

Ability description:

Built and rebuilt the storefront stack across Squarespace and Shopify, creating five end-to-end site redesigns while handling the operational layer behind the scenes. On the back end, I coordinated manufacturing across the US East and West coasts before expanding into the UK and China, and managed packaging, shipping, and customer fulfillment for orders reaching three continents.

Skills developed through this ability:

- E-commerce Operations

- Fulfillment Coordination

- Customer Experience Management

### Campaign Tracking & Iteration

Domain: data

Ability description:

Used platform analytics, mailing lists, storefront behavior, and campaign feedback loops to make SSMM more intelligent over time — what to launch, how to message it, where to push it, and what audiences were responding. That included maintaining Shopify, Mailchimp, and Google Analytics as the decision layer behind launches, promotions, post-purchase communication, and customer retention.

Skills developed through this ability:

- Performance Analytics

- Feedback Loop Optimization

- Campaign Strategy

### Manufacturing, Fulfillment & Logistics

- Managed production across the US West Coast and East Coast before expanding manufacturing relationships into the UK and China

- Organized packaging, shipping, and customer fulfillment for roughly 1,000 orders worldwide

- Translated a one-person brand into repeatable real-world operations across multiple production partners

- Used analytics to make launches smarter over time instead of relying on instinct alone

- Won the VVM Startup Accelerator Award, earning funding, mentorship, and business resources

- Received the Grinspoon Recognition Award for Entrepreneurial Spirit

- Used external validation to strengthen brand credibility beyond the immediate streetwear niche

- Proved the project had enough commercial and cultural traction to be taken seriously by startup institutions

## In Depth

#### The Graduation Photo that Started a Movement

One of our earliest supporters wore an SSMM hoodie under his graduation gown and took his entire set of graduation photos in it — cap, gown, tassel, and a brand nobody had heard of hiding underneath. Someone posted the photos with the caption "this boy got a bright future ahead of him," and within days it was circulating across dozens of meme pages, splitting comment sections between people laughing and people genuinely offended on the kid's behalf.

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney Fan wears SSMM Internet Tour Crewneck at his Graduation - photo meme that helped start SSMM meme marketing](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-memes_originals_1.jpg>)

That single post did something I didn't fully understand until later: it turned SSMM into a meme format rather than just a brand people wore. A second person wore SSMM in his yearbook photos, which spawned its own meme. Someone else wrapped their newborn baby brother in an SSMM hoodie and posted it, and the internet did the rest. I didn't write a single one of these memes — the audience did, on their own, unprompted.

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney Fan wears SSMM Internet Tour Crewneck at his Graduation - photo meme that helped start SSMM meme marketing](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-memes_originals_2.jpg>)

Looking back, this is where the meme marketing engine actually started. Not from a campaign I planned, but from fans finding ways to insert the brand into their own lives that were funnier and more absurd than anything I could have scripted. Every future giveaway and meme push was really just me trying to feed that same energy back to the community that had already proven it existed.

#### Baseball Cards for the Internet Age

At the peak of its run, I'd had the chance to meet and work with a growing list of names in the underground scene — Pouya, Fat Nick, Ghostemane, Lil Peep, TooPoor (Layla), Rae Sremmurd, and others. Somewhere in the middle of all that, an old childhood obsession resurfaced: I used to collect Yu-Gi-Oh cards, and something about the format stuck with me long after I'd stopped playing.

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney Clout Cards - The Baseball Cards of Internet Culture](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-cloutcards_1.jpg>)

I pitched an idea to our biggest supporters: free "Clout Card" booster packs inside every order. Each card followed the classic trading-card layout — a candid or funny photo of a rapper, musician, or influencer on the front, with a set of "superpowers" underneath describing, in a hyperbolic and slightly sarcastic tone, what that person was actually known for in real life.

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney Clout Card featuring Lil Peep](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-cloutcards_2.jpg>)

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney Clout Card featuring Matt Ox](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-cloutcards_3.jpg>)

What started as a joke between a handful of superfans grew into a full set — cards for the artists above, plus names like Gary Vee, Tai Lopez, and Ice Poseidon, and eventually cards for people inside the SSMM universe itself: our photographers, our models, and the meme pages that had helped build the brand's early audience. It turned every order into a small collectible moment, gave fans a reason to talk to each other about who they'd pulled, and folded the brand's own community into the same mythology as the celebrities it referenced.

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney Clout Card featuring Pouya](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-cloutcards_6.jpg>)

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney Clout Card featuring Tai Lopez and Gary Vaynerchuk](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-cloutcards_5.jpg>)

#### The Meeting I Missed to a Flat Tire

Not every connection worked out, and this one still stings. I'd lined up a meeting with Tycho Burwell, a director who went on to shoot music videos for artists like Nettspend and Trippie Redd. On the drive down, I got a flat tire — and because I young guy in the US without a phone plan, I had no way to call Tycho to explain, and no way to call my insurance for help either.

A state trooper happened to stop, realized how far over my head I was, and helped me change the tire himself. He was kind about it, but he also told me straight: don't push on to New York on a spare, turn around and go home. So I did — heartbroken, because there was no way to salvage the meeting from the side of a highway with no working phone.

Tycho took the no-show personally, and understandably so from where he was sitting — we never spoke again. It's a small story in the grand scheme of the brand, but it's an honest one: running something alone means the gap between "almost" and "actually" sometimes comes down to things completely outside your control, like a tire and a phone plan you couldn't yet afford.

#### Alone in Times Square with Two Suitcases Full of Clothes

My first solo trip to New York City was for a photoshoot. I had just moved to the US and barely knew my way around, and I drove three and a half hours from a small college town straight into Times Square traffic with two suitcases full of clothes in the back seat. I found street parking on a busy Brooklyn block — next to a fire hydrant, because it was the only open spot. Only later did I find out why fire hydrant spots aren't taken once I saw the ticket.

No food, no water, no local contacts, and a budget too tight to absorb surprises. But I met Alexis Conti, the photographer, and her model — who turned out to be an incredible musician in his own right. Alexis was great friends and the photographer for rising NYC rapper CASHRINA. So, I was quietly starstruck the entire shoot while trying to act like directing a shoot in Times Square was a completely normal Tuesday for me.

Despite every logistical thing working against it, the shoot itself was one of the best days of the brand's run. The photos from that day are still some of the strongest in SSMM's entire catalog — proof that resourcefulness and a good eye can outperform budget, connections, and experience combined.

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney New York City photoshoot](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-photoshoots_3.jpg>)

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney New York City photoshoot](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-photoshoots_4.jpg>)

Image: [SkipSchoolMakeMoney New York City photoshoot](<https://georgedreemer.com/public_img/ssmm/skipschoolmakemoney-photoshoots_5.jpg>)

# thoughtbubble — Knowledge-First Social Network

A knowledge-first social network, built from scratch by two self-taught developers. Just a love for web development, zero budget, launched in the USA and expanded to reach 900+ users across the world.

thoughtbubble was designed to shift social media away from entertainment toward sharing ideas, insights, and self-improvement content.

We built it to alpha in under a year, hand-coding every layer ourselves custom authentication, MySQL architecture, real-time notifications, and the full social product without a framework, CMS, or boilerplate.

## Experience Snapshot

thoughtbubble

**Role:** Co-Founder & Full-Stack Developer

**Type:** Social Network Startup

**Location:** Amherst, MA, United States

### Highlights

- Built full back-end in PHP + MySQL — database, API, and server-side logic

- Co-built front-end in HTML, CSS, and Javascript — AJAX interactions, dynamic content, and responsive design

- Built all social features — feed, posts, comments, likes, pins, notifications, and profiles

- Built registration, login, and account management system

- Collected and analyzed user data to improve engagement and retention

- Co-designed UX — feed, profiles, and post system

- Iterated on UI based on direct user feedback

- Presented product to investors and potential partners at local startup events

- Grew to 900+ registered users with zero ad spend

- Secured copyright for the platform and managed legal procedures

## In Depth

#### Built from scratch & self-taught

Nikolay and I built thoughtbubble in PHP, JavaScript, and MySQL. There was no framework, no CMS, no boilerplate — we'd hit wall after wall and just keep watching web development videos until it clicked. I built the full back-end of thoughtbubble and co-developed the front-end, while also designing the full icon set and logo in Adobe Illustrator.

I built the back-end systems below, and co-developed the front-end and social feed logic with Nikolay:

- Authentication and session management

- News feed with custom sorting logic

- Post types — text, photo, video

- Likes, pins, and comments

- Hashtags and categories

- Notifications

- Profile customisation and account settings

- A user feedback pipeline

We shipped 76 major updates between the closed alpha and public launch.

The infrastructure ran on shared hosting with a manually configured MySQL database. There was no version control beyond file backups, no CI, no staging environment. It was scrappy by any standard, but it worked.

We scaled to nearly a thousand users, and every line of it was ours. Every feature or bug fix was a new learning experience and a sleepless night.

#### The idea that was early

The pitch was simple: a social network where your feed only teaches you things. No vacation photos, no cat videos — just insights from books, actionable quotes, and self-improvement content. We built it inspired by the rise of Gary Vaynerchuk and Tai Lopez and the audiences forming around them. People were already sharing nuggets from books, videos, and articles — but existing platforms weren't built to hold that kind of content well. We saw a clear gap: entertainment-first platforms simply weren't built to support information-rich content.

So we set out to build something different. We envisioned posts where the UI would include things like book titles, author, and reference material. A category system built around four pillars of self-improvement: health, wealth, relationships, and fulfillment. The user profile would read more like a personal development journal — with pinned posts, categorized content, and a space for reflection.

What we were describing — a curated, knowledge-first feed with social mechanics — is close to what Twitter's long-form threads, Substack, and LinkedIn's creator-focused pivot eventually became. We were two self-taught devs with no funding and no network, so the timing didn't matter in the end. But the product instinct was right.

Looking at how much that space has grown, there's real satisfaction in knowing two founders with no prior experience, no funding, and no network saw it coming early. I sometimes wonder what we could have built with even a fraction of the resources those platforms eventually had — but that experience taught me that the desired outcome isn't always the best outcome. There's a deeper plan at work, and life had other things in store beyond scaling thoughtbubble to its full potential.

#### How we got 900 users without spending a dollar

We didn't run ads. We didn't have a budget. The growth strategy was entirely manual: reach out directly to people who were already creating self-improvement content on YouTube or Instagram, show them the platform, and get them to seed it with their content. We identified early that a knowledge-first feed is only as good as the content in it — if the first 50 users post junk, the product is dead on arrival.

We tracked registrations, session counts, and engagement metrics in MySQL and used those numbers to prioritise what to build next. The most-used features got more polish. The least-used ones got cut or rethought. We didn't call it a data-driven product loop at the time, but that's exactly what it was.

#### We got ripped off by a lawyer - got the copyright anyway

At some point, two first-time founders decided their app needed real legal protection — because apparently "two guys with a login page" doesn't hold up as a legal entity on its own. So we hired a copyright lawyer, nodded confidently at documents we barely understood, and paid real money to learn what a retainer is the hard way. He did the bare minimum, billed like he'd written us a constitution, and left us wondering if we'd just been the world's greenest, most polite scam victims.

Classic story. We pushed through it anyway, filed everything properly ourselves where we could, and got the copyright registered. It cost more than it should have and took longer than it should have — but it's ours, on paper, forever, which is more than I can say for the money we spent on that lawyer.

In hindsight, it was my first real lesson in the unglamorous side of building something — the admin, the fine print, the people who see inexperience as an opportunity rather than something to protect. Nobody warns you that "founding a startup" sometimes means arguing about an invoice with a man in a blazer. I'd handle it very differently now. But we got the copyright — and honestly, that's a better ending than most first-lawyer stories get.
